transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello Doctor. I guess... well, they told me I had to come in. It's my talking. They say my talking gets all mixed up. 

See, I work as a cleaner, a janitor, mostly the night shifts, and I try to explain things to people, just trying to get my point across, but... well, I try to explain about the keys. I have this huge ring of them for the building, all these heavy brass and silver keys clinking around against my leg, and I'll be explaining that, and then I start talking about the jail, because of the locks and the bars and being trapped, you know? It just makes sense to bring it up right then. And then I move on to the prayer rug, the one with the woven patterns and the tassels, and then the chess pieces—the knights and the bishops and how they move across the board—because it's all part of the exact same thing I'm trying to say. 

But people... they just stare at me. My supervisor, my sister, they just get this look on their face. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying at all. They say my words are just a big tangled mess, even though I'm just trying to explain the whole situation to them, from the keys right down to the chess board. I don't feel mixed up, but everyone else says they can't understand a lick of it. So, I guess that's why I'm sitting here today.

When you're explaining about the keys and then move to talking about the jail and the prayer rug and the chess pieces—do you see how those things are connected to each other, or do you realize that someone listening might not understand how they all fit together?

Well, see, that's exactly what I was just saying before. To me, the connections are as clear as day. Bright as those buzzing fluorescent lights in the hallways I mop at two in the morning. I mean, if you really stop and think about it... you have the keys, right? The heavy brass ones I carry. Keys lock things up. They keep people out, or they keep people in. Which is exactly what a jail does, it's a cage with bars. And when you're locked up in a cage, what else are you supposed to do? You pray to get out. You get down on your knees, maybe on a rug, a nice woven prayer rug with those little red and gold tassels on the ends, and you pray for a way out of the trap. And trying to find a way out... well, that's a strategy, isn't it? It's a game of moves and counter-moves, trying to outsmart the warden, just like moving the knights and the bishops across the black and white squares on a chess board. 

It's a straight line from one thing to the next! It makes perfect sense. But when I lay it all out for them, just like I did for you, step by step... they just shake their heads. Like I told you, they tell me my talking gets all mixed up and they cannot follow what I am saying. At all. 

I don't realize they aren't getting it until they give me that blank, heavy stare. Because in my head, I'm just telling them the plain truth about the building and the locks and the whole system of it all. I'm trying to give them the entire picture, from the keys in my hand right down to the chess pieces, and they just say it's a tangled mess. It's frustrating, Doctor, it really is. It makes my chest tight because I'm doing my best to explain how the world works and they act like I'm speaking a foreign language. They just don't see the lines connecting everything.

If I told you that keys, jails, prayer rugs, and chess pieces actually have nothing to do with each other—that they're just separate, unrelated objects—would you agree with me, or do you believe they truly are connected in some fundamental way?

No, no, I couldn't agree with that. I couldn't agree with that at all, Doctor, because... well, how could they not be connected? It's like you're asking me to look at a car and say the steering wheel has absolutely nothing to do with the tires. See, this is exactly what I've been trying to tell you. This is the whole entire reason they made me come sit in this office in the first place. Like I just said, what brings me here is that everyone insists my talking gets all mixed up. I try to explain it to them, I really try to break it down—about the heavy keys, and then the jail, and then the prayer rug, and then the chess pieces—and people tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. 

But to me, the fundamental way they connect is the only thing that actually makes any sense! If you take a key, you're locking a door, right? That's a jail. I see the iron bars in my head when I'm pushing my mop bucket down the linoleum on the third floor at work. And the floor tiles there, they're black and white, exactly like a chess board, and I'm walking across them like a knight, you know, two steps forward, one step over, just trying to figure out the grand strategy of it all. Trying to find a way out, praying for an answer on that woven rug. 

So when you sit there and tell me they are separate, unrelated objects... well, that just tells me you're doing the exact same thing my sister does, and my supervisor. You're just looking at the surface of things. You aren't seeing the wires pulling everything together. And that's... well, I guess that's why everybody says my words are just a big mess. Because I'm seeing the whole giant machine, how every piece turns the next piece, and you're all just looking at one little gear and telling me the other gears don't exist. It just goes round and round, and I try to explain it, from the keys straight through to the chess, and nobody follows it. They just give me that look.

Have you always seen these connections between the keys, the jail, the prayer rug, and the chess pieces? Or did you start noticing these connections more recently—maybe over the last few weeks or months?

Well, no, not always. Not my whole life, if that's what you're asking. Let me think... it's been... well, if I really track it back, it's been about two years and five months. Right around there. Two years and five months. Because I remember exactly when the whole picture finally came together for me and the wires all lit up. 

It was right after this... well, this incident. A complete misunderstanding at the building where I work. See, I was just doing my rounds, checking the doors like I'm supposed to, making sure the heavy brass locks were secure, and somebody got the entirely wrong idea about why I was in the east wing at that hour. They blew the whole thing way out of proportion, made a mountain out of a molehill, and the police got involved. There was this brief detention. Just a brief one! But they put me in the car and took me down to the station, and I was sitting there in that holding area... and that's when it happened. 

I was sitting there, and I really looked at the bars. The jail. And I heard the officer's keys clinking on his belt, sounding just like my keys, and it all just clicked into place. Before that night, two years and five months ago, I was just pushing a broom and mopping the linoleum, not seeing the grand strategy of the chess board, not understanding why a person might need a woven rug to pray for a way out of the trap. But after they locked me in there over a simple misunderstanding at the building... well, ever since then, I can't unsee it. 

I try to tell my supervisor that the misunderstanding was actually a blessing because it showed me how the keys and the jail and everything else actually connect, but he just interrupts me. People are always interrupting before I can get to the most important part of the story, Doctor, which is how that brief detention changed everything. Because if they hadn't misunderstood what I was doing with the keys that night, I might never have seen how the whole giant machine works, you know? I might still just be walking on the black and white tiles without realizing I'm a knight on the board. So it's been two years and five months of finally seeing the truth of it all.
Besides seeing things in your head like the iron bars and the chess board, do you ever hear voices or sounds that other people around you don't seem to hear?

Well... you know, it's funny you bring that up, because... yes. Yes, I do. And it's not just a random sound, Doctor, it's not just the building settling or the pipes clanking. It's a voice. A very specific voice. 

I'll be working, you know, pushing my cart down the hall, doing my job, minding my own business. The building is empty, mostly. Just the hum of the HVAC system and the squeak of my rubber soles on the floor. But then, I'll be near the air vents—the big metal ones near the baseboards on the second floor, the ones with the thick iron grates—or maybe I'll just be in the mop closet in the back, ringing out the strings of the mop, just trying to get the dirty water down the drain. And I'll hear him. 

It's a man's voice. Deep, kind of echoing just a little bit out of the ductwork or bouncing off the cinderblock walls in the closet. And he says my name. He just calls out my name, or he tells me... he tells me that I ruined everything. "You ruined everything," he says. Just like that. 

And I always stop what I'm doing. I freeze right there with my hands on the plastic wringer, because I look around, expecting to see my supervisor or one of the night guards standing right there in the room with me. Because it sounds so real, Doctor. It's not like a memory or a thought bouncing around inside my skull. It sounds as real as you sitting right across from me right now. It sounds exactly like someone is standing right beside me, practically breathing on my shoulder. 

I'll go out into the hallway and look both ways, checking all the doors, looking at the locks. Nothing. Nobody there. Just those bright lights buzzing. But the voice, it comes right out of the vents. Or from behind the big gallon jugs of floor wax in the mop closet. "You ruined everything." And I try to figure out what he means, you know? What did I ruin? Was it the grand strategy? Was it the situation with the police two years ago? I try to ask him, I speak right back into the vent, but he just says it again. And I've asked the other guys on the night shift if they heard someone yelling, I say, "Did you hear that guy shouting from the ductwork?" And they just give me that same blank, heavy stare I was telling you about. They don't hear a thing. But I know what I hear. It's a real man's voice, standing right there with me in the dark, telling me I ruined it all, and nobody else seems to notice him at all.

When your supervisor or sister tells you that the keys and the jail and the prayer rug and the chess pieces are not actually connected to each other—do you think there's any possibility they might be right, or are you completely certain that they are connected no matter what anyone tells you?

Am I certain? Doctor, I... I am completely, one hundred percent certain. There is no possibility they are right. None at all. Because they don't see what I see, or maybe they just don't want to admit it. 

See, they try to pull the wool over my eyes all the time. My supervisor, he actually tried to prove me wrong once, to prove that I was just making connections out of thin air, but it really just proved how deep the whole thing goes. Let me tell you exactly what happened, because this is important, this really shows you what I'm dealing with every single night on that shift. 

He took me down to the security office—you know, the one down by the loading dock where it always smells like diesel exhaust, with all the monitors on the wall, all those little glowing squares. He sat me down in this squeaky rolling chair and he pulled up the playback from the third-floor corridor. He points his thick finger at the screen and he says, "Look, look right here, there's nothing there, nobody is doing anything." He was trying to tell me I was just imagining the whole setup. 

But even when my supervisor showed me nothing was on the camera, I knew. I still felt absolutely sure of it. Because a cheap security camera doesn't catch the real truth, Doctor. It doesn't catch how the building people have marked me. They marked me, probably right after that brief detention I told you about. I know they did. And they use the hallway lights—you know how those long fluorescent tubes have that little flicker before they buzz on, that sort of stutter? They use that. It's a signal. They use the hallway lights and these little looks they give each other to warn each other about me. 

I'll be emptying the wastebaskets in the accounting department, just tying off the clear plastic bags and putting in new liners, minding my own business, and I see them out of the corner of my eye. One of the guys in a nice suit will look over at the receptionist, just a tiny little dart of the eyes, a little look, and then the light above my cart buzzes and flickers. They're warning each other. They're saying, "There he is, watch out for him." 

So when my supervisor points at a grainy video screen and says there's no connection, that everything is separate and I'm just getting mixed up... well, it just makes me realize he's either completely blind to the machine or he's in on it too. He has to be. Because how could you not see it? The lights, the looks, the heavy keys, the floor tiles... you can't just tell me it's not real when I am living right in the middle of it. No matter what anyone tells me, no matter how many times my sister sighs at me, I know exactly what's going on. I'm certain of it.

During your work shifts, do you ever find yourself frozen in place, unable to move, or do you sometimes feel like your body won't respond the way you want it to? Or do you ever hold the same position for a long time without meaning to?

Frozen? No, no, I don't get frozen. I mean, earlier I said I freeze when I hear that man's voice coming out of the air vents, but that's just me stopping to listen, you know? Like a deer in the headlights, just holding my breath and trying to figure out exactly where the sound is coming from. It's not like my body actually gets stuck or I can't move my arms or legs. My body does exactly what I tell it to do. 

It has to, Doctor, because this is a very physical line of work. You can't just be standing around like a statue when you have the entire east wing to finish before 4:00 AM. Have you ever operated an industrial floor buffer? The big rotary ones with the heavy pads? You absolutely cannot freeze up when you're running one of those, or the torque will pull you right across the linoleum and smash you straight into the drywall. You have to use your whole body, your shoulders, your back, just leaning into the machine to keep it steady and sweeping it side to side. I'm fifty-three years old, but I'm in good shape because I'm always moving. I'm always pushing that heavy yellow cleaning cart—the one with the squeaky front left wheel that I keep writing work orders for, but maintenance never fixes it. They probably leave it broken on purpose, to be honest with you, so they can hear me coming down the hall. 

So, no, I don't ever hold a position without meaning to. I'm not like one of those street performers painted silver down by the park, just standing there without blinking. If I am standing perfectly still in the middle of a corridor, holding my mop or my rag, it's strictly on purpose. It's because I'm observing the board. I'm watching the accountants' desks, or I'm waiting to see if that fluorescent tube is going to do its little stutter-flicker thing to signal the others. But my muscles work just fine. I can step away whenever I want. 

You have to stay agile, see? Because if you realize you're a knight on the chess board, you have to be ready to make your move, jump over the other pieces if you have to. You can't be glued to the black and white tiles when the people in the suits are giving each other those looks. So no, my body never gets stuck or stops responding. Even when my lower back aches from hauling the heavy trash bags out to the dumpster by the loading dock, I keep moving. I always keep moving.

When you're standing still in the hallway observing the board, as you just described—if someone came up and gently moved your arm or repositioned your body into a different stance, would your arm stay in that new position, or would it fall back down naturally?

If someone moved my arm? Why would... why would anyone do that, Doctor? I mean, first of all, nobody touches me. People in that building, the accountants, the managers in their expensive suits, they look right through me like I'm made of glass, unless they want to complain about a smudge on the glass doors by the lobby. They certainly aren't coming up and repositioning my limbs like I'm some sort of... some sort of store mannequin in a window display at Macy's. 

But let's just say, hypothetically, someone did that. Let's say one of the night guards, maybe Frank—he's the one with the heavy boots who always leaves his half-empty coffee cups balanced right on the edge of the trash can instead of just throwing them inside, which drives me absolutely crazy, by the way—let's say Frank came up and grabbed my arm and lifted it up. I'd pull it right back down! Or it would just drop. I wouldn't just leave it hanging up in the air. That doesn't even make any sense. My muscles are my muscles. If I'm not holding my arm up to scrub a stubborn coffee stain off the wall or to reach up and dust the top of a doorframe, gravity is just going to take it right back down to my side. 

I'm not made of clay, Doctor. I'm flesh and bone. If someone lifted my arm, it's going right back down the second they let go, or the second I yank it away from them, because I don't like people in my personal space anyway. Especially not when I'm trying to concentrate on the board. You have to understand, when I'm standing there in the hallway, I'm calculating. I'm reading the black and white tiles, I'm watching the fluorescent lights for that flicker, and I need my hands ready. I usually have my hands resting right on the handle of the mop bucket anyway, the big yellow plastic one, so if someone tried to move my arm, they'd have to pry my fingers off the grip first. So no, it definitely wouldn't stay in some new position. It would just fall right back to where it naturally belongs. I don't even know why you'd think my arm would just stay stuck like that.

When you're standing still in that hallway observing the board, and you're concentrating hard on the lights and the signals—do you ever notice that your muscles feel stiff or rigid, like they're locked up? Or does your body feel completely normal and relaxed?

Stiff? Locked up? No, no, Doctor, I don't... my muscles don't get locked up at all. I mean, sure, I'm fifty-three years old, so if you're asking if my lower back gets a little tight after hauling garbage for six hours, well, yeah, of course it does. But when I'm standing there in the hallway, observing the board and watching the tiles? No, my muscles feel completely normal. Loose, even. 

Well, maybe not relaxed like I'm taking a nap on a beach somewhere, because you absolutely cannot let your guard down when they're sending signals right over your head. You have to stay alert. But physically? My body is just doing exactly what it's supposed to do. I'm usually just leaning a little bit on my mop handle—it's this yellow fiberglass handle, see, they used to be wood but they swapped them all out last year because the wood ones were splintering and one of the day-shift guys got a nasty piece of pine stuck right in the meat of his palm. So I lean on the fiberglass handle, just taking the weight off my feet for a minute, because I wear these thick rubber-soled work shoes that the uniform catalog says are orthopedic, but let me tell you, after you've been walking on poured concrete and commercial linoleum since nine o'clock at night, your arches are going to burn no matter what kind of shoes you're wearing. 

So I'm just standing there, and my muscles are totally loose. They have to be loose, Doctor. Think about it. If you're locked up stiff like a statue, you can't react. If I see that little stutter-flicker from the overhead lights, or if I notice one of the late-night accountants shifting his desk phone exactly two inches to the left—which is a move they make, by the way, right before the night guard does his third-floor rounds—I need to be able to move instantly. I need to be able to pivot, push my cart into the nearest alcove, or just start wiping down a glass partition so I look like I'm just doing my job. If my muscles were rigid, if I was all locked up, I'd be a sitting duck out there in the open corridor. 

So no, I don't feel stiff at all. My shoulders might ache from lifting those giant trash bags out of the breakroom bins—people just dump whole half-full cups of coffee and soda in there, and the liquid pools at the bottom of the bag and makes it weigh an absolute ton—but that's just regular tired, you know? That's just working for a living. I'm completely in control. I just stand there, breathing quiet, keeping my knees slightly bent. You never lock your knees anyway, or you'll pass out. I learned that back in gym class before I left high school. You always keep a little bend in the knee, like a shortstop waiting for the pitch. So that's what I do. No stiffness, no locking up. Just waiting, watching the board, completely ready for whatever move they try to make next.

You mentioned you lean on your mop handle and keep your knees slightly bent while you're observing. If you were standing like that for a long time, and I came over and gently straightened your leg out, would your leg stay straight in that stretched position, or would it naturally bend back to where you had it?

Doc, I really don't understand why you keep asking if people are coming up and moving my limbs around like I'm a puppet on a string. It's just... it's just not something that happens on the night shift. But okay, if you came over and straightened my leg out while I was leaning on my mop? No, it absolutely wouldn't stay straight. It would go right back to being bent, immediately. 

I mean, think about it. If you straighten my leg, you're throwing off my whole center of gravity. I've got my hands on the fiberglass handle, I've got my weight distributed so my lower back doesn't spasm, and if you lock my knee out, I'm either going to tip over or I'm going to pull it right back to where I had it so I don't lose my balance. Like I was saying before about locking your knees—I actually saw a kid do that once, back in... I think it was tenth grade? Right before I left school to start working full-time. We were having this assembly in the gymnasium, standing on those heavy wooden bleachers that pull out from the wall, and this kid, Tommy or Timmy something, he locked his knees standing up in the back row. Passed out cold, pitched straight forward, and took out two girls in the row in front of him. It was a whole disaster, the school nurse had to come running with the smelling salts and everything. 

So I never lock my legs. Never. If you straightened it, I'd bend it right back. My body isn't going to just freeze in some awkward, stretched-out position. That doesn't make any sense physically. My muscles are going to recoil, like a spring, right back into that shortstop stance. I have to stay grounded. If the fluorescent lights start doing that sequence, the... the three short flickers and the one long one, I need to be able to push off that back foot and get moving down the corridor. If my leg is just stuck out straight because someone messed with it, I'd be completely off balance, and they'd catch me right there on the open tiles. So no, it would just naturally bend right back to where I need it to be. My body is totally normal, it just does what I need it to do so I can stay one step ahead.
If I lifted your arm up to shoulder height right now and let go, would your arm stay up there in the air for a while, or would it immediately drop back down to your side?

Doctor, I feel like we're just going in circles with this now. Are we really back to the mannequin thing? Like I just said, if you lift my arm up and let go, it's dropping straight back down. Immediately. Boom. Right back to my side, exactly where it started. 

I mean, look at me. I've been hauling wet garbage, pushing mop buckets, and wrestling with a commercial floor buffer for twenty years. Do you know what those industrial floor buffers are like? The big heavy ones with the thick rotating pads? You have to practically fight those things to keep them from swinging wide and taking chunks out of the drywall. The vibration alone just rattles right up your arms and settles deep into your rotator cuffs. After a six-hour shift of that, my shoulders are completely shot. They feel like they're filled with lead. So if you lift my arm up to shoulder height, there is absolutely zero chance it's just going to float there in the air like I'm directing traffic. It's going to fall like a sack of wet towels the absolute second you take your hand away. 

Besides, gravity works on me exactly the same way it works on everyone else. I don't have some kind of magic anti-gravity muscles. If I'm not actively using my brain to tell my arm, 'Hey, hold this spray bottle up to the glass,' then the arm goes down. That's just basic biology. I learned that much before I even left high school. You don't expend energy you don't need to expend, especially not on the night shift when you need to conserve your strength for when the lights start doing their sequence. If my arm was just hanging up in the air for no reason, not only would it ache like crazy, but I'd look completely ridiculous, and the absolute last thing you want to do when the floor managers are sending signals is draw attention to yourself by standing in the middle of the hallway with your arm pointing at nothing. 

So no, Doctor. It wouldn't stay up for a while. It wouldn't stay up for even a second. You let go, it drops. It's just flesh and bone, and it goes right back down to my pocket where it belongs.

Doctor, I'd like to try something with your permission. I'm going to gently lift your arm up to shoulder height and hold it there for just a moment. I want to see if your arm stays in that position or if it falls back down. Is that okay with you?

I mean... fine. Yeah, you can try it, Doc. Go ahead. You have my permission. If you really need to prove it to yourself, you can come over here and lift my arm. But I'm telling you right now, it’s going to do exactly what I just spent the last five minutes explaining to you—it’s going to drop right back down to my side. 

You can hold it there for a moment, you can hold it there for ten minutes if you really want to stand there and do that, but the absolute second you pull your hands away, gravity is taking over. Especially on this right side—assuming you're going to grab the right one, since I'm right-handed—because that rotator cuff is completely fried anyway. I was telling you about that industrial floor buffer, right? When you're swinging that massive thing back and forth across the main lobby, especially over by the glass doors where the tile gets slick from people tracking in the rain and the mud, you have to tense your whole upper body just to keep the machine from spinning out of your hands and smashing into the security desk. So my shoulder is already aching right now, just sitting here in this chair talking to you. 

So yeah, you can lift it. But don't be surprised when it drops like a sack of rocks. I just... I really don't get why we're so hung up on this. I'm sitting here trying to explain to you about the signals, the stutter-flicker in the overheads, how I have to stay alert and keep my knees bent so I'm ready to move when the floor managers start shifting things around, and you want to play 'Simon Says' with my limbs like I'm some kind of window display. It just doesn't make any sense to me. But look, if doing this little test gets us moving on to something else, then sure, come on over and lift the arm. Just be gentle with the joint, like I said, it’s got twenty years of commercial cleaning wear and tear on it. And just... don't try to lock my knee out next, alright? Because I already told you what happens when you do that, and I'm not looking to pass out on your floor today.
I'm going to lift your arm up to shoulder height now and then let go. I want you to just relax and let me see what happens. Ready?

Yeah, I'm ready. Just... remember what I said about the joint, okay? Don't force it past where it naturally stops, because right about shoulder height is where that pinching starts from wrestling with that floor buffer. But yeah, I'm relaxing it. Just letting it hang completely loose. Go ahead. 

Yep, there it is. You got it? Okay, and... see? Boom. Right back down. Smacked right into my thigh, exactly like I told you it would. 

I mean, I really don't know what you were expecting, Doc, like it was going to magically float up there pointing at the ceiling tiles? It's just a tired arm. It's a fifty-three-year-old arm that's hauled way too many heavy yellow mop buckets full of dirty water. Honestly, if you took all the miles of linoleum I've covered on the night shift over the years and laid them out end to end, I bet I've walked from here to Chicago and back. You don't do that kind of mileage and end up with arms that just hover in mid-air for no reason. Gravity always wins. Always. Unless I'm actively flexing my muscles to hold up a bottle of industrial glass cleaner to wipe down the lobby doors, it's going down. That's just how the physical world works. 

So... I mean, are we done with the mannequin test now? Because I really feel like we're wasting a lot of time on this when we should be talking about the signals. The floor managers aren't waiting around while we play these little gravity games with my shoulder. When those overhead lights do the three short and one long flicker, I need to know you actually understand what that means for the corridor shifts. That's what's actually important here, not whether my arm falls down when you let go of it.
When I lifted your arm just now, did you feel any resistance in your muscles, like they were pushing back against my hand? Or did your arm feel completely floppy and easy to move?

Resistance? Pushing back? No, Doc, I wasn't pushing back at all. I mean, why would I? You told me to relax, so I relaxed. It was completely floppy, just dead weight in your hands. 

Like I was saying before, you try hauling those heavy-duty commercial trash bags out to the loading dock dumpsters every night for twenty years, and believe me, your arms aren't going to have any secret energy left to fight back against somebody just lifting them up. It felt exactly like when you pick up a giant string mop head that's been soaking in the bucket all night—just heavy, wet, and limp. There was absolutely zero resistance. I didn't feel my muscles doing anything, honestly. They were just along for the ride. You lifted it, it went up, you let go, it went down. Simple as that. No pushing, no pulling, no nothing. 

But see, this is exactly what I mean about us going in circles here. We just spent all this time proving my arm is just a regular, tired, floppy arm, and meanwhile, the overheads in the east corridor are probably doing their sequence right now. I keep trying to tell you, the floor managers use that specific flicker—the three short, one long—to signal when the hallway layout is going to shift. If I'm sitting here analyzing whether my rotator cuff pushed back against your hand by a fraction of an inch, I'm missing the pattern. And if you miss the pattern, you get caught in the shift, and you do not want to be in the wrong section when they change the walls around. 

So, no, there was no resistance, Doc. Just a tired, floppy arm that does exactly what gravity tells it to do. Can we please, finally get back to the lights now? Because I really need you to understand how the signals work before the night shift starts, and we are burning daylight on these little muscle tests.

When I was holding your arm up at shoulder height, before I let it go—did your arm feel like it was in any particular position, or did it feel completely limp and like it had no strength to hold itself in any shape at all?

I mean... no, Doc, it didn't feel like it was in any shape at all. I really don't know how many different ways I can explain the exact same thing to you. It was just completely limp. Dead weight. Like I said before, it's just a tired arm. 

When you were holding it up there, I wasn't... I wasn't secretly flexing or trying to pose like a statue or something. It just felt like a heavy piece of meat hanging off my shoulder joint. You ever try to hold up a soaking wet industrial mop head by just one of the strings? It doesn't hold a shape, right? It just sags down, heavy and wet and useless until you wring it out in the press. That's exactly how my arm felt. Just completely empty of any strength to hold itself up. If your hand wasn't under my wrist, it wouldn't have been up there for even a split second. It was just hanging there, waiting for you to let go so it could drop.

But look, I really... I really gotta say, I am getting pretty frustrated with all these questions about my arm. We're spending twenty minutes dissecting exactly how my elbow felt in mid-air, and it has absolutely nothing to do with what I came in here to tell you about. You keep asking about muscles and resistance and shapes, and I keep trying to tell you that none of that matters when the corridors start shifting. If I'm sitting around worrying about whether my arm is floppy or stiff, I'm going to miss the sequence.
